cells.tense: Right now, in what you're carrying, you can hold weight without going rigid, and the floor stays steady under you.
cells.act: stay in contact while it is hard
cells.ask: Something in your care is wobbling this week. Stay near it — or near whoever is holding it — without stepping back and without taking it over. Keep showing up while it's unsteady.
cells.core:
Right now, you can hold what has to be held and stay soft in it at once. You don't grip to make the load lighter, and you don't let go to make it easier on yourself. People stand on that floor without ever being told it's there. That's the whole of what you do with it.

Something in your care is about to come down — maybe a structure you built, maybe one you only leaned on. When it falls, don't brace and don't rush to pick it back up. Sit with whoever is in it. You might think staying near means fixing. It doesn't. You can feel the weight alongside someone and keep your own feet under your own chair. That is the practice. What you cannot hold, you don't have to carry for them.
cells.sheetLine: You can hold the weight and stay soft doing it.
cells.place: at the sudden clearing, where the false structure falls away

cells.tense: You're bracing for something that hasn't happened yet, holding it so hard the holding itself is becoming the load.
cells.act: adjust the share until it is fair, then stop
cells.ask: Look at the load you're carrying that isn't yours alone. Adjust the share — give back the part that belongs to someone else, keep what's yours — and once it's fair, stop.
cells.core:
Something in your care may come down, and you've decided to keep it up by strength alone. Your grip is doing what a brace does — it holds, and it can't let anything move. What was steady in you is getting stiff, and the stiffness reads as strength. It's the arm holding the wall so the wall doesn't have to hold itself.

Not every structure deserves the weight of your whole body, and your arm isn't what keeps anyone honest. Shift what you are carrying until the load is fairly split, then stop shifting. Some people will mind that you stopped reaching first. A few will ask why the posture changed. Tell them what's actually true about it, plainly, and leave the answer with them.
cells.sheetLine: You're keeping something up that wants to come down.
cells.place: at the sudden clearing, where the false structure falls away

cells.tense: There was pressure, and you let go of what you were holding, and nothing in you has reached for anything solid since.
cells.act: stop holding what no longer serves
cells.ask: Notice what you're still half-carrying that you already decided to stop carrying. Set that down — not everything, just the one that's already finished. Nothing gets concluded by setting it down.
cells.core:
When the weight came, holding it felt like more than you could do, so you stopped holding. What used to be yours to carry, you now set down before it starts. The door behind you already closed. You're still in front of it. Nothing about that says anything about what you're made of.

You don't need to pick up the whole thing again. That isn't what this is asking. There is something you have already decided to stop carrying, and your hands haven't gotten the message yet. Put that down. Nothing has to be concluded by setting it down. If it turns out you want it back, you can pick it up. Your hands will have told you something in the meantime.
cells.sheetLine: You put things down before they get heavy.
cells.place: at the sudden clearing, where the false structure falls away

cells.tense: You're holding something steady right now, and if someone said so you'd credit luck, or the situation, or anyone but your own grip.
cells.act: move toward the thing you actually want
cells.ask: Take one small step this week toward something you'd want a year from now. No plan, no announcement to anyone. Just the one step, and nothing has to be committed by taking it.
cells.core:
You're holding something steady right now, and you don't count it. The steady thing might be a job, a routine, a person you keep showing up for. From the outside, it looks like backbone. From the inside, it doesn't register as anything you're doing. When you come apart, the same holds — it gets filed under circumstances.

Go to wanting, before the load. At some point something pulled you toward a version of your life, and you turned without naming it a decision. Take one small step this week toward something you'd want a year from now. No plan and no announcement. The step is small enough that nothing has to be committed by taking it. If it goes nowhere, you'll have learned that. If it goes somewhere, you'll have found the thing your strength is for.
cells.sheetLine: The steady thing is you, not the luck.
cells.place: at the sudden clearing, where the false structure falls away

attempts.check: The record says 'collapse under pressure — holding feels too dangerous' for Too Little, but I cannot say what happened there or when, so the core locates the person at the closed door without narrating the loss. A reader could reasonably object that bracing for a future collapse and being past holding are not opposites — but they are two faces of one capacity: gripping what cannot be gripped, and never gripping again. The persistence ask (status 2) survives my read being wrong: it just carries the chosen direction one more week and reports what holds, useful either way. The sentence that serves me more than the person is 'the structure was never yours,' which flatters the reader at the person's expense — cut.
